target: Teh di sini otomatis manis, kalau mau tanpa gula, minta teh tawar.
english: Tea here is automatically sweet — if you want it sugarless, ask for teh tawar.
tip: Tawar = plain, unsweetened (and also 'to bargain'): teh tawar = unsweetened tea.

target: Bangun tidur, dia langsung mengecek HP-nya.
english: As soon as he wakes up, he immediately checks his phone.
tip: HP (say ha-pe) is the everyday word for phone; ponsel sounds formal. Mengecek HP = check the phone.

target: Setiap malam dia memasang alarm di HP sebelum tidur.
english: Every night she sets the alarm on her phone before sleeping.
tip: Setting an alarm is pasang (or setel): pasang alarm jam lima = set a 5 a.m. alarm.

target: Mbak, boleh minta password wifi-nya, ya?
english: Miss, could I have the wifi password, please?
tip: Boleh minta + the thing is the all-purpose polite request – no 'may I have' verb chain needed: boleh minta password wifi-nya. The closing ya softens it further.

target: Baterainya habis, saya harus ngecas HP dulu.
english: The battery is dead, I have to charge my phone first.
tip: Ngecas puts the casual nge- prefix on the borrowed root cas (from 'charge'). Loanwords take Indonesian prefixes freely – and every generation says ngecas HP.

target: Boleh saya numpang ngecas HP di sini sebentar?
english: May I charge my phone here for a moment?
tip: Numpang = politely use someone's facility: numpang ngecas = charge here, if I may.

target: HP saya dicas semalaman, tapi baterainya tetap cepat habis.
english: My phone was charged all night, but the battery still drains fast.
tip: Even a borrowed root takes the passive di-: cas (charge) becomes dicas = gets charged. HP saya dicas = my phone was charged – no 'was' word needed.

target: Baterai HP saya tinggal sepuluh persen, sebentar lagi mati.
english: My phone battery is down to ten percent; it will die soon.
tip: Tinggal usually means 'live, stay', but before an amount it means what's left: tinggal sepuluh persen = only ten percent remaining. Context picks the meaning.

target: Saya baru mengunduh aplikasi untuk belajar bahasa Indonesia.
english: I just downloaded an app for learning Indonesian.
tip: Mengunduh = download; in speech people also just say download: download aplikasinya.

target: Aplikasi belanja itu sering memberi diskon besar.
english: That shopping app often gives big discounts.
tip: Diskon is the everyday word; potongan harga is what the poster says.

target: Kakak memakai aplikasi untuk mencatat pengeluaran setiap bulan.
english: My older sister uses an app to record her expenses every month.
tip: Pengeluaran is built on keluar (go out): expenses are literally 'the going-out' of money. Its mirror is pemasukan, income – money coming in (masuk).

target: Kantor kami memakai aplikasi khusus untuk absen setiap pagi.
english: Our office uses a special app for clocking in every morning.
tip: Absen in Indonesia = to mark attendance (clock in), not to be absent.

target: Naik ojol lebih cepat daripada naik mobil kalau jalanan macet.
english: Taking an ojol is faster than going by car when the roads are jammed.
tip: Ojol = short for ojek online, the app-booked motorbike taxi everyone uses.

target: Tanpa aplikasi peta, saya pasti tersesat di kota sebesar ini.
english: Without a map app, I would definitely get lost in a city this big.
tip: Ter- for accidents: tersesat = to get lost (not on purpose), from sesat.

target: Waktu video call, sinyal di rumah nenek sering putus-putus.
english: During video calls, the signal at grandma's house often keeps cutting out.
tip: Doubling turns a one-off into an on-and-off: putus = cut off, putus-putus = keeps cutting out. Sering putus-putus (often cutting out) is the classic bad-connection complaint.

target: Kami video call dengan tim Jakarta setiap Senin pagi.
english: We video-call the Jakarta team every Monday morning.
tip: English loans work as verbs with nothing added: kami video call – no melakukan, no verb ending. Same with meeting, chat, and upload in office talk.

target: Dia lupa mematikan mikrofon waktu rapat online tadi pagi.
english: He forgot to turn off his microphone during the online meeting this morning.
tip: Mematikan is literally 'make dead': mati (dead) + me-...-kan. Turning off the mikrofon means killing it – the same logic English uses in 'kill the lights'.

target: Foto-foto liburan kami tersimpan di HP dan juga di laptop.
english: Our vacation photos are stored on the phone and also on the laptop.
tip: Ter- + simpan = stative: tersimpan = (safely) stored, with no one doing the storing.

target: Pesan di grup RT pagi ini penting, tolong dibaca.
english: The message in the neighborhood group this morning is important; please read it.
tip: RT (rukun tetangga) = your neighborhood block; nearly every RT has its own grup.

target: Om dan tante paling rajin mengirim gambar selamat pagi di grup.
english: Uncles and aunts are the most diligent at sending good-morning images in the group.
tip: Gambar selamat pagi – flowery good-morning images – are a daily ritual in Indonesian family chat groups, sent most faithfully by om dan tante.

target: Berita di grup itu belum tentu benar, cek dulu sebelum percaya.
english: News in that group is not necessarily true; check first before believing it.
tip: Belum tentu is literally 'not yet certain': belum tentu benar = not necessarily true. Indonesian prefers belum (not yet) where English says a flat 'not'.

target: Stiker lucu itu dikirim adik saya ke semua grup.
english: That funny sticker was sent by my little sister to all the groups.
tip: Passive di- + agent, no 'oleh' needed: dikirim adik saya = sent by my little sister.

target: Lokasi restorannya saya kirim lewat pesan, ya.
english: I'll send the restaurant's location by message, okay?
tip: Object first + saya kirim = everyday passive: lokasinya saya kirim = I'll send the location.

target: Sinyal di kampung halaman saya sekarang sudah kuat.
english: The signal in my hometown is strong now.
tip: Kampung halaman is a fixed pair meaning your family's hometown – where you're from, not just any village. Plain kampung can be any village or neighborhood.

target: Saya lupa password email lama, jadi membuat akun baru.
english: I forgot my old email password, so I made a new account.
tip: Password is the everyday word; kata sandi is what formal screens call it.

target: Internet di sini lambat, mengunggah video saja butuh satu jam.
english: The internet here is slow; just uploading a video takes an hour.
tip: Mengunggah = upload and mengunduh = download are near-twins that are easy to swap. Casual speech dodges the problem: people say upload and download as-is.

target: Indonesia punya ribuan pulau, dari Sabang sampai Merauke.
english: Indonesia has thousands of islands, from Sabang to Merauke.
tip: Dari Sabang sampai Merauke = 'all across Indonesia' – Sabang is the country's far western tip, Merauke its far eastern one. The set phrase for the whole nation.

target: Nelayan berangkat melaut sebelum matahari terbit setiap pagi.
english: The fishermen set out to sea before sunrise every morning.
tip: The me- prefix can turn a noun into a verb: laut (sea) becomes melaut, to head out to sea – which is what nelayan (fishermen) do every morning.

target: Petani mulai memanen padi di sawah minggu depan.
english: The farmers start harvesting the rice in the fields next week.
tip: Rice has three names: padi in the field, beras raw in the bag, nasi cooked on your plate.

target: Kami menginap di desa kecil di kaki gunung berapi.
english: We stayed overnight in a small village at the foot of a volcano.
tip: Ber- can mean 'having': gunung berapi is literally a mountain having api (fire) – a volcano. The fire is built right into the word.
